query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a refractory high-entropy alloy with a baseline composition optimized for high-temperature performance, reducing the content of fast-diffusing elements (e.g., Ti) and increasing the content of slower-diffusing, oxide-forming elements (e.g., Cr, Ta, and Al) will promote the selective formation and retention of a continuous, protective CrTaO4 (possibly with dispersed Cr2O3 and Al2O3) oxide layer by limiting outward cation flux relative to inward oxygen diffusion.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory or high-temperature HEA (e.g., an alloy akin to NV1 from PMC6513993) in a homogenized, polycrystalline state with a baseline composition that includes trace Ti and enriched Cr, Ta, and Al.
generation.intervention: Synthesize two sets of HEAs: one with a reduced Ti content (optimized composition) and a controlled variant with slightly higher Ti content (by, for example, 50–75% increase) while keeping other elements constant.
generation.conditions: Expose both alloy variants to isothermal oxidation tests at high temperatures (e.g., 1100 °C in air) for extended durations (exceeding 100 hours) to capture steady-state oxidation kinetics.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer (with minor contributions from Cr2O3 and Al2O3) at the alloy surface that acts as a diffusion barrier.
generation.mechanism: Differential cation diffusion kinetics govern selective oxidation; reducing fast-diffusing elements (like Ti) minimizes disruptive cation flux, thereby enabling slower-diffusing species (Cr, Ta, Al) to form a continuous and coherent oxide scale that retards both outward metal diffusion and inward oxygen transport.
generation.predicted_outcome: The optimized (low-Ti) alloy will exhibit a parabolic oxidation kinetics curve with a significantly lower mass gain (e.g., on the order of 50% lower) relative to the high-Ti variant. Microstructural characterization should reveal a continuous, adhesive oxide layer in the optimized alloy versus a more porous, discontinuous scale in the variant with higher Ti.
generation.baseline: The high-Ti alloy variant serving as the control that is expected to form a less protective, heterogeneous oxide scale resulting from increased cation mobility and discontinuous oxide formation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies under high-temperature, isothermal oxidation conditions (e.g., >1000 °C in air) and for HEA systems where the key oxide-forming elements (Cr, Ta, Al) are present in sufficient amounts; deviations in oxygen partial pressure or cyclic oxidation conditions might lead to different behaviors.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties include the precise quantitative impact of variations in Ti versus the contributions of other elements, possible interactions with microstructural features (e.g., grain size, segregations), and phase stability of the oxide scale over extended periods.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy batches: one with the optimized low-Ti composition and one with an intentionally elevated Ti content while keeping all other elements constant. Subject both batches to identical isothermal oxidation treatments at 1100 °C in air for 200 hours. Use thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) to record mass gain and employ cross-sectional SEM/EDS and XRD to evaluate oxide layer continuity and phase composition.
measurements: Mass gain curves (to identify parabolic vs. non-protective kinetics)
Cross-sectional imaging to assess oxide layer continuity and thickness
Phase identification of the oxide scale via XRD and possibly TEM/EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-Ti alloy exhibits an oxide layer that is equally continuous and protective, with similar mass gain kinetics and oxidation resistance as the low-Ti optimized alloy, then the hypothesis that reduced Ti and differential cation diffusion govern protective oxide formation is falsified.

Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions. AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm2, which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. At 1100 oC, NV1 alloy outperformed all 3 other alloys (AlCrMoNbTi, (AlCrMoNbTi)0.99Si0.01, and AlCrMoTaTi) within 48 hours. The main difference in the composition of NV1 alloy was 75% less Ti comparing to AlCrMoNbTi, (AlCrMoNbTi)0.99Si0.01, and AlCrMoTaTi. Since CrTaO4 layer played a major role in reducing the oxidation of NV1 alloy, it is very likely that the reduced Ti content of NV1 alloy promoted the formation of CrTaO4 layer, leading to enhanced oxidation resistance at 1100 °C. These previous works suggested that parabolic mass gain rate observed for the oxidation of RHEAs/RCCAs could be attributed to the formation of protective Al2O3 and Cr2O3 on the alloy surface, although no detailed microstructural characterization were shown in these studies,. The oxidation kinetics changed according to the content of Al initially from a parabolic (Mn15Al5) to a logarithmic (Mn10Al10 and Mn5Al15) rate, caused by the formation of a protective layer of Al2O3 instead of the MnxOy oxidic layer observed in the case of the first-mentioned alloy. Moreover, the sub-surface oxidation and porosity caused by the Mn diffusion toward the oxide layer were completely suppressed from 10 at.% of Al, reducing the overall thickness of the oxide layer from ≈25 μm (Mn15Al5) down to ≈1 μm. Considering the above-stated, changing the content of Al can be used for precise tailoring of the complex performance of the prepared alloys to achieve desired properties not only at the laboratory but also at elevated temperatures.

papers.title: An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide.
papers.system: Refractory high-entropy alloy (NV1) with reduced Ti content
papers.approach: Long-term isothermal oxidation tests (up to 200 h) at 1000 °C and 1100 °C with thermogravimetric analysis, XRD and microstructural characterization
papers.findings: At 1100 °C the alloy exhibited a two-stage parabolic weight gain; formation of a continuous CrTaO4-based oxide layer (with dispersed Al2O3 and Cr2O3) improved oxidation resistance compared to similar alloys. At 1000 °C the kinetics were exponential, indicating a less protective oxide scale.
papers.mechanism: Selective oxidation promoted by reduced Ti content favors the formation of a dense, continuous CrTaO4-based oxide that retards both outward cation diffusion and inward oxygen diffusion.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Insights into the Oxidation Mechanisms of CrMnFeCoNi High-Entropy Alloy Using In Situ X-ray Diffraction.
papers.approach: In situ high-temperature XRD and densitometric analysis during oxidation in air (and comparison with vacuum conditions)
papers.findings: A graded oxide layer develops featuring an outer Mn-rich region and an inner Cr-rich region. The formation and evolution of oxides, with phase changes (e.g., Mn2O3 to Mn3O4), correlate with the expected differential diffusion sequence of Mn > Cr > Fe > Co > Ni.
papers.mechanism: Differential cation diffusion rates govern the oxide-layer stratification, where faster-diffusing species (e.g., Mn) form outer, generally non-protective oxides and slower diffusing species (e.g., Cr) accumulate to form inner oxides that can serve as partial barriers.

papers.title: Modeling Oxidation of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Using Stochastic Cellular Automata.
papers.approach: Mesoscale modeling via stochastic cellular automata incorporating thermodynamics, kinetics, and reconstructed microstructural features
papers.findings: Simulations reproduced oxide scale growth with primary formation of α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3 under diffusion-controlled (parabolic) kinetics; microstructure (e.g., grain boundaries) was shown to strongly influence the spatial distribution and continuity of the oxide scales.
papers.mechanism: Coupled effects of elemental diffusivities, thermodynamic stability, and microstructural heterogeneity govern whether a protective, continuous oxide scale develops.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Advanced experimental techniques including in situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure analysis to monitor oxidation at relatively low temperatures
papers.findings: A layered oxide structure forms on the alloy surface with distinct compositional zones (e.g., Ni-rich pre-oxide, followed by Cr2O3 and then a multi-oxide layer rich in Fe, Co, and Mn); the sequence correlates with each element’s redox potential, atomic size, and diffusivity.
papers.mechanism: A combination of thermodynamic propensity (redox potentials) and kinetic factors (diffusivity and atomic size) dictates which oxides form where; proper balance can yield a protective layer by localizing slower-diffusing and stable phases (e.g., Cr2O3 or Al2O3) at the metal/oxide interface.

papers.title: Influence of the Al Content on the Properties of Mechanically Alloyed CoCrFeNiMnXAl20-X High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: CoCrFeNiMnAl high-entropy alloys with varying Al content
papers.approach: Systematic variation of Al content followed by high-temperature oxidation tests at 800 °C with kinetic analyses and cross-sectional microstructural examination
papers.findings: Alloys with higher Al content (e.g., Mn5Al15 and Mn10Al10) formed dense, thin, and protective oxide layers dominated by Al2O3, displaying logarithmic kinetics versus thicker, less protective Mn-rich oxide scales in low-Al alloys.
papers.mechanism: Al addition promotes the formation of a continuous, stable Al2O3 scale that acts as an effective barrier against oxygen ingress, contrasting with non-protective oxides when Al is deficient.

papers.title: Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with ultrafine grain structure
papers.approach: Processing by stationary friction to refine grain size followed by high-temperature oxidation tests (850–1050 °C) and microstructural analysis of oxide layers
papers.findings: Ultrafine-grained samples exhibited reduced oxidation kinetics (12–48% reduction in mass gain) compared with coarse-grained, attributed to the formation of more uniform and continuous oxide scales (predominantly chromia and alumina) due to enhanced grain-boundary diffusion.
papers.mechanism: The increased density of grain boundaries facilitates controlled, uniform diffusion of oxide-forming species, resulting in a denser and more protective oxide scale that slows further oxidation.

established: Protective oxide layers (such as CrTaO4, Al2O3, and Cr2O3) can form on HEAs under high-temperature oxidation, reducing further oxygen ingress.
Elemental diffusion kinetics and microstructural features (e.g., grain boundaries) are critical in governing the oxidation behavior.
Selective oxidation driven by alloy composition modifications (e.g., reduced Ti or increased Al content) can promote the formation of more protective oxide scales.
Oxidation kinetics often follow diffusion-controlled (parabolic) or logarithmic regimes when protective scales are formed.

approaches_tried.approach: Long-term isothermal oxidation tests with thermogravimetric analysis
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated that small compositional changes (e.g., reduced Ti) result in the formation of continuous, protective CrTaO4-based oxide layers.

approaches_tried.approach: In situ high-temperature XRD and densitometry in varying oxygen pressures
approaches_tried.outcome: Identified graded oxide layer formation driven by differential diffusion of elements; established sequence and phase evolution.

approaches_tried.approach: Stochastic cellular automata modeling incorporating microstructural features
approaches_tried.outcome: Predicted oxide scale growth and the role of microstructure in enabling formation of protective oxides.

approaches_tried.approach: Systematic alloying (varying Al content) with subsequent oxidation testing
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated that higher Al contents yield denser, protective Al2O3 scales, suppressing detrimental sub-surface oxidation.
Enhanced oxidation resistance due to increased grain boundary density leading to a more uniform oxide layer.

mechanisms: Selective oxidation driven by elemental composition that promotes formation of specific oxides (e.g., CrTaO4, Al2O3) which act as barriers.
Differential diffusion of alloying elements, leading to layered oxide structures where slower-diffusing species capitalize on forming protective scales.
Grain boundary facilitated diffusion enhancing the uniformity and continuity of the protective oxide layer.
Interplay of redox potential, atomic size, and cohesive energies dictating the sequence and stability of oxide formation.
disagreements: The role of certain elements (e.g., Ti) is debated: while reduced Ti can promote protective CrTaO4 formation in some studies, other reports indicate titanium may participate in forming complex, less-protective oxides.
Observed oxide species can vary between studies (e.g., presence or absence of a continuous Cr2O3 layer), suggesting that microstructural and kinetic nuances lead to different outcomes.
The balance between thermodynamic predictions (e.g., ThermoCalc outputs) and experimental findings (such as unexpected oxide phase evolution) remains a point of contention.
open_questions: What are the precise kinetic thresholds (in terms of diffusion rates and elemental fluxes) that dictate the transition from non-protective to protective oxide scale formation on HEAs?
How does the interplay of grain boundary density and specific alloying additions quantitatively influence the formation and stability of protective oxides in long-term high-temperature exposures?
What are the limits of protective oxide scale formation under variable oxygen partial pressures or cyclic oxidation conditions?
How do subtle changes in elemental ratios alter the nucleation and growth modes of oxide layers, and how can these be measured in situ at the atomic scale?
opportunities: Design experiments that directly compare HEAs with incremental variations in key elements (e.g., Al, Ti, Cr) while controlling for grain size, to quantitatively measure differences in oxide scale formation kinetics and continuity.
Leverage in situ microscopic and spectroscopic techniques (e.g., atom probe tomography during oxidation) to directly observe diffusion pathways and oxide layer evolution at the nanoscale.
Combine advanced computational models with controlled experimental studies to reconcile thermodynamic predictions with kinetic measurements in protective oxide formation.

Investigate the effects of oxygen partial pressure and temperature cycling on the long-term stability of the protective oxide layer, potentially revealing critical failure modes that could falsify a protective layer mechanism hypothesis.

directions.direction: Modify the alloy composition to promote selective oxidation. For example, reducing elements (like Ti) that may hinder the formation of protective oxides and enriching elements (such as Cr, Ta, and Al) that form slow‐growing, continuous oxides.
directions.assessment: This approach directly addresses the mechanistic hypothesis by focusing on how alloying elements govern selective oxidation. Prior evidence (e.g., PMC6513993 and PMC9692591) supports that reduced Ti content promotes continuous CrTaO4 (and related Cr and Al oxides) formation. The physics of selective oxidation via varying cation diffusivities is well established, and controlled compositional tweaks are highly feasible in high-entropy alloy (HEA) synthesis.

directions.direction: Refine the alloy’s microstructure through thermomechanical processing. Grain refinement increases grain boundary density, which can provide uniform diffusion pathways for oxide-forming ions and enhance the continuity of the protective scale.
directions.assessment: While microstructural control affects oxidation kinetics by altering effective diffusivities (as shown in PMC9026100), it is an indirect intervention. It respects thermal exposure constraints and is supported by observations of ultrafine-grained HEAs exhibiting lower oxidation rates. However, it may not isolate the key chemical diffusion effects governing oxide formation.

directions.direction: Conduct in situ high-temperature surface characterization (e.g., HTXRD, in situ TEM) to directly observe the nucleation and growth of oxide scales.
directions.assessment: This strategy can yield real-time kinetic data and validate the diffusion-controlled formation of protective oxide layers. Although it is an excellent diagnostic technique, it primarily confirms the existing hypothesis rather than intervening to control the phenomenon.

directions.direction: Develop a mesoscale computational model that incorporates thermodynamic and kinetic parameters (element-specific diffusion coefficients, redox potentials) to predict the growth of protective oxide scales.
directions.assessment: Simulation can capture the differential diffusion of elements and its influence on oxide layer formation. The approach is supported by previous stochastic cellular automata studies (e.g., PMC9498035), but its predictions require experimental validation and might be limited in capturing all microstructural nuances.

directions.direction: Apply a surface treatment or coating to mimic the protective oxide, then compare with the uncoated HEA to deduce the inherent oxide formation mechanism.
directions.assessment: While applying protective coatings can improve oxidation resistance, it does not answer the intrinsic mechanistic question of how HEAs naturally develop protective oxide layers. It provides a controlled baseline but may confound the self-forming protective mechanism in the alloy.

choice.direction: Composition design to promote selective oxidation via differential cation diffusion.
choice.why: This direction directly tests how the controlled alloy chemistry governs the formation and retention of a continuous protective oxide layer. By comparing alloys with minor compositional variations (especially in Ti, Cr, Ta, and Al content), one can directly observe the effect on oxide continuity and protectiveness. The approach is supported by multiple studies (e.g., PMC6513993, PMC9692591) that indicate reduced Ti content and optimized Cr/Al levels enable the formation of continuous protective scales.
